blocks.en: Hello, young explorers, and welcome back to Michael's Morning Listening!
Today our first story begins with one photo on a phone, and with footprints that waited one hundred and twenty million years to be found.
Then we dive into an ancient sea to meet the fattest little squid of Jurassic times.
Ready?
Let's go!
Our story starts in Phu Phrabat National Park in Thailand.
A visitor named Pichai was walking along a small stream when he saw strange, deep marks pressed into the sandstone beside the path.
The marks looked like giant footprints.
He took a photo with his phone and posted it online with a question: "Do these look like dinosaur footprints to you?"
Park rangers came the very next day to measure the marks.
Then dinosaur experts studied them carefully — and confirmed the exciting news.
The marks are real!
They are six footprints of a meat-eating dinosaur, made about one hundred and twenty million years ago.
There is no skeleton and no bones in the rock — only footprints, like a short message the dinosaur left behind.
The soft ground kept the prints, the rock preserved them, and the stream hid them for ages.
Only when the water went down did the footprints appear again.
Scientists believe the dinosaur was walking here long ago, perhaps looking for food or water.
One walk, one photo — and a dinosaur stepped back into the world!
Now let's meet the belemnites — squid cousins from the time of the dinosaurs.
They are extinct today, but their hard inner shells turned into fossils, and scientists find them all over the world.
Most belemnite fossils are thin and pointed, like little bullets, only one or two centimetres wide.
But in Wyoming, in the United States, scientists found a very different one.
Its name is Wyoteuthis, and it lived about one hundred and sixty million years ago, in Jurassic seas.
Its shell was shaped like a little barrel — and six centimetres wide!
That makes it the fattest, chunkiest belemnite ever found.
In real life, the animal was about sixty centimetres long.
A team from the University of Manchester studied the funny fossil.
Some scientists even joke that fossils like this look like "squid butts".
A fat little squid, a silly nickname — and a real puzzle for science: why did this one grow so wide, when all its cousins stayed slim?
Here's today's idiom: "follow in someone's footsteps."
If you follow in someone's footsteps, you do the same job or the same things as a person who came before you — just like walking in the footprints they left in the ground.
The rangers in our story followed in the dinosaur's footsteps, step by step, footprint by footprint!
Here is an example: "Lucy's grandmother was a great scientist, and Lucy wants to follow in her footsteps one day."
Whose footsteps would you like to follow in?
Let's think about today's stories.
We followed a dinosaur's footprints in Thailand, and we met the fattest little squid of the Jurassic seas.
Now here are two questions for you.
First: if you found strange, giant footprints beside a stream, what would you do — run away, or take a photo and call a scientist?
Second: when you grow up, whose footsteps would you like to follow in?
Talk about it with your family!
That's all for today, young explorers.
Keep your eyes open on every walk — you never know what is waiting quietly in the rocks under your feet.
See you tomorrow morning!
